title: Raga Vadhans
hookLine: a raga that opens with peacocks in the rain and holds both wedding songs and laments

cards: Monsoon rain on a tin roof. Peacocks calling from the fields, that sharp, high cry that carries a long way. That's the first sound Raga Vadhans makes in the Guru Granth Sahib.
Its opening hymn, by Guru Nanak, begins with the peacocks singing and a voice telling her sister that the rainy season of Sawan has come. Joy, color, wet earth.
And yet, further into the same raga, there are songs for a wedding and songs for the dead, side by side.

teach.h: PEACOCKS, SISTER, THE RAINS HAVE COME.
teach.b: Start with the peacocks. In the opening hymn of Vadhans, in plain English, the peacocks call sweetly: sister, the rainy season has come.
In this hymn the rains are the season of love; the bride hears them and thinks of her Husband Lord. It's yesterday's longing, but the night has given way to rain and color. Now turn the pages.

teach.h: GHORIAN: SONGS OF THE WEDDING HORSE.
teach.b: Later in Vadhans, Guru Ram Das wrote ghorian, songs of the wedding horse.
In Punjabi custom, ghorian are sung as the groom sets out on his mare, and the Guru's ghorian take that joyful scene and make it about the soul riding toward God.
Further on, Guru Nanak wrote alahnian, laments, the songs of mourning sung for the dead.
A wedding and a funeral, in one raga. That's not a mistake in the filing. Both are moments when a life crosses a threshold: a bride or groom leaving one home for another, a soul leaving this world.
The Gurus set both to the same music.
The raga doesn't pick a side between joy and grief; it holds them both. And the Granth turns both toward God. The wedding becomes the soul's union with the Lord.
The lament sets the loss inside the Creator's order. Tomorrow, a closer look at one of each.

how: Shabads in Vadhans are sung in that raga in kirtan; Guru Ram Das's ghorian are linked with wedding occasions, and Guru Nanak's alahnian, laments, are linked with mourning.

practice: Open one hand and bring to mind something glad from this year, a birth, a wedding, a good day; open the other and bring to mind a loss, large or small, and let each rest where it is.

Don't trade one for the other; just hold both, and breathe between them. If you pray, say Waheguru over both hands. If a loss feels heavier than you can hold, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.
